questions.text: The chemical potential of component $i$ is defined as:
questions.detailed: $\mu_i$ is the partial molar Gibbs energy: the change in $G$ when a tiny amount of $i$ is added at constant $T,P$ and fixed amounts of the other components. $\mu_i = (\partial G/\partial n_i)_{T,P,n_{j\neq i}}$.

questions.text: For a multicomponent system with several phases at thermodynamic equilibrium, what condition applies to a component present in more than one phase?

options.label: a
options.text: Its chemical potential is equal in every coexisting phase in which the component is present.

options.label: b
options.text: Its chemical potential is zero in every phase, regardless of composition.

options.label: c
options.text: Its chemical potential is equal across the coexisting phases only when their compositions are identical.

options.label: d
options.text: Its chemical potential is highest in whichever phase has the greatest density.

questions.keyExplanation: At equilibrium, the chemical potential of each component is equal between all phases in which that component can exchange. The phases need not have the same composition.
questions.concise: Phase equilibrium requires equality of each component's chemical potential across coexisting phases.
questions.detailed: For each component i, equilibrium requires $\mu_i^\alpha=\mu_i^\beta$ across phases that can exchange that component. The condition is equality of chemical potential, not zero chemical potential, identical phase composition or a rule based on density.

questions.text: The Gibbs–Duhem equation at constant $T$ and $P$ is:
questions.detailed: $\sum_i n_i\,d\mu_i=0$ (or $\sum_i x_i\,d\mu_i=0$) at constant $T,P$. It means the chemical potentials of the components in a solution are not independent — fix one and the rest are constrained.

questions.text: Raoult's law for the solvent $A$ in an ideal solution is:
questions.detailed: Raoult's law: $p_A=x_A P_A^\circ$, i.e. the partial vapour pressure is proportional to the mole fraction, with the pure-component vapour pressure as the proportionality constant. It is the ideal-solution reference ($\gamma_A=1$).

questions.text: Henry's law for a dilute solute $B$ is written as:
questions.detailed: In the dilute limit $p_B=K_H x_B$, with $K_H$ an empirical Henry constant (not the pure vapour pressure). Henry's law is the reference for the *solute*, Raoult's for the *solvent*.

questions.text: Choose the correct option:
questions.assertion: If the solute B obeys Henry's law over a range of compositions, the solvent A must obey Raoult's law over the same range.
questions.reason: The Gibbs–Duhem equation links the changes in chemical potentials of all components in a solution.

options.label: a
options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

options.label: b
options.text: A is true but R is false

options.label: c
options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

options.label: d
options.text: A is false but R is true

questions.detailed: This is a classic use of Gibbs–Duhem: $\sum x_i\,d\mu_i=0$. If the solute's vapour pressure follows $p_B=K_H x_B$, integrating the Gibbs–Duhem constraint forces the solvent to obey Raoult's law ($p_A=x_A P_A^\circ$) over that range. So R explains A.

questions.text: The activity of a component is defined (Raoultian reference) as:
questions.detailed: $a_i=p_i/p_i^\circ$: the ratio of the actual vapour pressure to that of the pure component. For an ideal solution $p_i=x_i p_i^\circ$ so $a_i=x_i$. Activity is the "effective" mole fraction.

questions.text: The activity coefficient $\gamma_i$ is defined by the relation:
questions.detailed: $a_i=\gamma_i x_i$, so $\gamma_i=a_i/x_i$. For an ideal solution $\gamma_i=1$; $\gamma_i>1$ indicates positive deviation from Raoult's law (weaker A–B attraction), $\gamma_i<1$ negative deviation.

questions.text: At $x_A=0.40$, the vapour pressure of A over a solution is $30\ \mathrm{mmHg}$. If $P_A^\circ=100\ \mathrm{mmHg}$, the activity and activity coefficient of A are:
questions.detailed: $a_A=p_A/p_A^\circ=30/100=0.30$. Then $\gamma_A=a_A/x_A=0.30/0.40=0.75$. A value below 1 means negative deviation from Raoult's law (A–B attractions stronger than average).

questions.text: Fugacity is introduced because:

options.label: b
options.text: Real gases do not follow $p$ as their effective escaping tendency

options.label: d
options.text: It is a measure of entropy

questions.detailed: For a real gas the chemical potential is $\mu=\mu^\circ+RT\ln a$, but $a$ is not simply $P$. Fugacity $f$ is the "corrected pressure" such that $\mu=\mu^\circ+RT\ln(f/f^\circ)$ holds at all pressures. For an ideal gas $f=P$; in general $f=\phi P$, where $\phi$ is the fugacity coefficient.

questions.text: For an ideal gas, the fugacity coefficient $\phi=f/P$ equals:
questions.detailed: For an ideal gas $f=P$, so $\phi=1$. Deviations of $\phi$ from unity measure non-ideality; as $P\to0$, $\phi\to1$ for all gases.

questions.text: The chemical potential of an ideal gas at pressure $P$ is:
questions.detailed: Integrating $d\mu=V\,dP$ with $V=RT/P$ gives $\mu=\mu^\circ+RT\ln(P/P^\circ)$. For real gases replace $P$ by $f$. The $RT\ln$ form is the backbone of equilibrium and activity calculations.

questions.text: The partial molar volume $V_i$ of a component is defined as:
questions.detailed: $V_i=(\partial V/\partial n_i)_{T,P,n_j}$: the change in total volume when a small amount of $i$ is added. In general $V_i$ differs from the pure-component molar volume, and $V=\sum n_i V_i$.

questions.text: For component $i$ with activity $a_i=0.10$ at $500\ \mathrm{K}$, the relative partial molar Gibbs energy $\mu_i-\mu_i^\circ=RT\ln a_i$ is about:
questions.detailed: $RT\ln a_i=8.314\times500\times\ln(0.10)=4157\times(-2.303)\approx-9570\ \mathrm{J}\approx-9.6\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. A low activity lowers the chemical potential below the standard state.

questions.text: Which statements about activities are correct?
questions.detailed: All three hold. A pure liquid/solid has $a=1$ by the Raoultian convention (I); ideal solutions obey $a_i=x_i$ (II); and since $a=p/p^\circ$ it is a ratio and hence dimensionless (III).

questions.text: The tangent-intercept method applied to a plot of molar Gibbs energy $G_m$ versus $x_B$ gives:

options.label: d
options.text: The partial molar Gibbs energies $\mu_A$ and $\mu_B$ as the intercepts

questions.detailed: Drawing the tangent to the $G_m$–$x_B$ curve at a given composition and extending it to $x_B=0$ and $x_B=1$ yields $\mu_A$ and $\mu_B$ (the intercepts). This geometric trick is central to reading phase diagrams from free-energy curves.

questions.text: A solute follows Henry's law with $K_H=600\ \mathrm{mmHg}$. At $x_B=0.02$, its partial pressure is:
questions.detailed: $p_B=K_H x_B=600\times0.02=12\ \mathrm{mmHg}$. Henry's law is linear in the dilute region; $K_H$ is found from the slope of $p_B$ vs $x_B$ as $x_B\to0$.

questions.text: At the melting point of a pure substance, the condition relating the two phases is:
questions.detailed: At equilibrium the solid and liquid have equal chemical potential, $\mu_s=\mu_l$, which is equivalent to $\Delta G_{\text{fus}}=0$. Below $T_m$, $\mu_s<\mu_l$ (solid stable); above, $\mu_l<\mu_s$ (liquid stable).

questions.text: Which statement correctly distinguishes Raoultian and Henryan standard states for a component in a solution?

options.label: a
options.text: The Raoultian reference is the infinitely dilute limit; the Henryan reference is the pure-component state.

options.label: b
options.text: Raoultian uses the pure-component reference as $x_i\to1$; Henryan uses the dilute-limit reference extrapolated from $x_i\to0$.

options.label: c
options.text: The two standards use the same reference composition; they differ only in the numerical value of the activity coefficient.

options.label: d
options.text: Raoultian standard states are defined only for liquids, while Henryan standard states are defined only for gases.

questions.keyExplanation: The distinction is the reference composition: the pure-component limit for Raoultian activity and the hypothetical dilute-limit reference for Henryan activity.
questions.concise: Raoultian references the pure component; Henryan references the infinitely dilute limit.
questions.detailed: In a Raoultian standard state, the activity approaches the mole fraction and the pure-component reference is recovered as $x_i\to1$. In a Henryan standard state, the dilute-solution behaviour is extrapolated to define a hypothetical reference as $x_i\to0$. The difference is not simply a gas-versus-solid distinction.

questions.text: For a binary solution, suppose the solute activity is known as a function of composition. Which statement best describes what the Gibbs–Duhem relation permits you to infer about the solvent activity?

options.label: a
options.text: The solvent activity is always $1-a_B$, at every composition, whether or not the solution is ideal.

options.label: b
options.text: The two activities are independent because the solvent and solute use different standard states.

options.label: c
options.text: At fixed temperature and pressure, Gibbs–Duhem couples the differential changes of the two activities.

options.label: d
options.text: The activities must be equal whenever the solute obeys Henry's law and the solvent obeys Raoult's law.

questions.keyExplanation: For a binary solution at fixed temperature and pressure, $x_A d\ln a_A+x_B d\ln a_B=0$. The relation constrains activity changes across composition; it does not imply $a_A+a_B=1$ or equal activities.
questions.concise: Gibbs–Duhem links the differential changes in the two activities across composition.
questions.detailed: For a binary solution at fixed temperature and pressure, the Gibbs–Duhem relation is $x_A d\ln a_A+x_B d\ln a_B=0$. If one activity function is known over a composition range, this differential relation and an appropriate reference condition constrain the other. A single activity value at one composition is not enough by itself to determine an entire solvent-activity curve; neither the sum nor the values of the two activities must be equal.

questions.text: "The chemical potential is the same as the partial molar Gibbs energy."
questions.detailed: True. $\mu_i=(\partial G/\partial n_i)_{T,P,n_j}$ is by definition the partial molar Gibbs energy. It is also the partial molar quantity controlling phase and chemical equilibrium.

questions.text: For a real gas, the chemical potential is written as $\mu=\mu^\circ+RT\ln(f/f^\circ)$. As $P\rightarrow0$:

options.label: a
options.text: $f\rightarrow P$, so ideal-gas behaviour is recovered

questions.detailed: At low pressure all gases become ideal, so $f\to P$ and $\phi\to1$. Fugacity therefore reduces to pressure in the ideal-gas limit, and the $RT\ln$ expression smoothly recovers $\mu=\mu^\circ+RT\ln(P/P^\circ)$.

questions.text: Which of the following is *not* a partial molar quantity?
questions.detailed: Partial molar quantities are per-mole contributions of a component to an extensive property ($\bar V_i,\bar H_i,\mu_i=\bar G_i$, etc.). Total pressure $P$ is an intensive state variable, not a partial molar quantity.

questions.text: For an ideal solution with $x_A=0.25$ and pure vapour pressure $P_A^\circ=200\ \mathrm{mmHg}$, the partial pressure of A and the total pressure (if B is non-volatile) are:
questions.detailed: $p_A=x_A P_A^\circ=0.25\times200=50\ \mathrm{mmHg}$. With B non-volatile, the total pressure equals $p_A=50\ \mathrm{mmHg}$. Raoult's law lowers the solvent vapour pressure by dilution.

questions.text: The integral property $G=\sum n_i\mu_i$ is obtained from the partial molar quantities by:

options.label: b
options.text: Summing partial molar contributions weighted by mole numbers

questions.detailed: $G=\sum_i n_i\mu_i$. In general any extensive property $X=\sum_i n_i\bar X_i$. This additivity, combined with Gibbs–Duhem ($\sum n_i\,d\mu_i=0$), lets one go back and forth between integral and partial quantities.

questions.text: Positive deviation from Raoult's law ($\gamma_i>1$) usually indicates:

options.label: c
options.text: A–B interactions weaker than A–A and B–B interactions

questions.detailed: If unlike neighbours attract each other less strongly than like pairs, molecules escape more readily than ideal, so $p_i>x_i p_i^\circ$, $a_i>x_i$, $\gamma_i>1$ — positive deviation (e.g. many metallic systems showing a miscibility gap). The opposite gives negative deviation and possible compound formation.

questions.text: If $\bar G_B=RT\ln a_B$ relative to the standard state and $RT=8314\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}}$ at $1000\ \mathrm{K}$ with $a_B=0.01$, then $\mu_B-\mu_B^\circ$ is about:
questions.detailed: $8314\times\ln(0.01)=8314\times(-4.605)\approx-38{,}300\ \mathrm{J}=-38.3\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. Dilute solutes have strongly negative relative chemical potentials.
